title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 834–836 (Night 184, continuing nights-183), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 184 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Resolved to ask his father for the sleeping girl in the morning, Qamar al-Zamān bends to kiss her, then holds back, ashamed before God and suspecting that his father has set her beside him to test him and is watching from hiding. He touches her no further, but draws a precious ring from her little finger, engraved with three lines of love verse, puts it on his own, turns his back and sleeps. Maymūna praises his restraint to Dahnash and Qashqash, then turns herself into a flea and bites Budūr below the navel. Budūr wakes to find a young man of matchless beauty asleep beside her, praised in five lines of verse, and is seized by love. Dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ وَالثَّمَانُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿatu wa-al-thamānūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourth and-the-eighty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and eighty-fourth night,
sentences.n: al-rābiʿa, “the fourth”, agrees with al-layla, and the tens, al-thamānūna, follow in the same nominative case. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِى أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ قَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ وَاللَّهِ إِنِّي أُصْبِحُ وَأَقُولُ لِأَبِي زَوِّجْنِى بِهَا لِأَ تَمَلَّى بِهَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni qāla fī nafsihi wa-Allāhi innī uṣbiḥu wa-aqūlu li-abī zawwijnī bihā li-a tamallā bihā
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān said in himself: By-God, I, I-shall-rise-in-the-morning and-say to-my-father, ‘Marry-me to-her,’ that-I-may-take-my-fill with-her,
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān said to himself, “By God, in the morning I shall say to my father, ‘Marry me to her,’ so that I may take my fill of her;
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the story with Qamar al-Zamān's resolve from the end of the last night. wa-Allāhi, “by God”: wa- of the oath, with the genitive. uṣbiḥu, from aṣbaḥa, Form IV, “to be (or do a thing) in the morning”: “I shall rise and say”. li-, “to”, marks the one spoken to. zawwaja, Form II, takes bi- for the bride: zawwijnī bihā, “marry me to her”; the shadda of زوّجنى is the print's own, and its ى is the edition's ى for final ي. لا تملّى بها is doubtful. It is read here as in the last night, one word split by the print's spacing: li-atamallā bihā, “that I may take my fill of her”, li-, “so that”, with the subjunctive, and tamallā, Form V, with bi- of what is enjoyed. This time the print sets a shadda on the lām, which suits tamallā, and the same verb comes again in the next sentence, wa-atamallā bi-ḥusnihā, set whole. Setting the printed shadda aside, the letters could also be lā tumlī bihā, “do not keep me waiting for her”, but that needs a stretched sense.

sentences.t: وَلَا أَتْرُكُ نِصْفَ النَّهَارِ يَفُوتُ حَتَّى أَفُوزَ بِوِصَالِهَا وَأَتَمَلَّى بِحُسْنِهَا وَجَمَالِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lā atruku niṣfa al-nahāri yafūtu ḥattā afūza bi-wiṣālihā wa-atamallā bi-ḥusnihā wa-jamālihā
sentences.l: and-not I-will-leave half (of) the-day passing until I-win with-union-with-her and-take-my-fill with-her-beauty and-her-loveliness.
sentences.i: and I will not let half the day go by before I have won union with her and taken my fill of her beauty and loveliness.”
sentences.n: atruku niṣfa al-nahāri yafūtu, “I leave half the day passing”: taraka with an object and a verb describing it is “to let (something) do”. ḥattā, “until”, takes the subjunctive, afūza; atamallā is coordinated with it and is subjunctive too, though a verb ending in -ā shows no change. fāza bi-, “to win, attain”: bi- marks the prize. wiṣāl, union with the beloved. tamallā bi-, “to take one's fill of”: bi- marks what is enjoyed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ مَالَ إِلَى بُدُورَ لِيُقَبِّلَهَا فَارْتَعَدَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ الْجِنِّيَّةُ وَخَجِلَتْ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni māla ilā Budūra li-yuqabbilahā fa-irtaʿadat Maymūnatu al-jinniyyatu wa-khajilat
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān leaned to Budūr to-kiss-her; and-trembled Maymūna the-jinniyya, and-was-abashed.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān bent over Budūr to kiss her, and Maymūna the jinniyya trembled and was put to shame.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then (indeed)”, the narrator's usual link: inna puts its subject, Qamara, in the accusative. māla ilā, “to lean towards”. li-, “so as to”, with the subjunctive yuqabbila; the shadda of يقبّلها is the print's own. Budūr is a diptote: Budūra after ilā. irtaʿada, Form VIII, “to tremble”. khajila, “to be abashed, ashamed”. The jinn are watching to see which of the two sleepers is the fairer, and the youth's eagerness for the girl counts against Maymūna's side of the wager.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا الْعِفْرِيتُ دَهْنَشُ فَإِنَّهُ طَارَ مِنَ الْفَرَحِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā al-ʿifrītu Dahnashu fa-innahu ṭāra mina al-faraḥi
sentences.l: And-as-for the-ʿifrīt Dahnash, then-indeed-he flew from the-joy.
sentences.i: As for the ʿifrīt Dahnash, he flew for joy.
sentences.n: ammā … fa-, “as for … (then)”: the fa- brings in what is said about him. ṭāra mina al-faraḥi, “he flew from joy”: min gives the cause. Of a jinnī the phrase can be taken literally as well as in its usual sense, “he was beside himself with joy”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا أَرَادَ أَنْ يُقَبِّلَهَا فِي فَمِهَا اسْتَحَى مِنَ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَدَارَ بِرَأْسِهِ وَأَلْفَتَ وَجْهَهُ وَقَالَ لِقَلْبِهِ اصْبِرْ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā arāda an yuqabbilahā fī famihā istaḥā mina Allāhi taʿālā wa-dāra bi-raʾsihi wa-alfata wajhahu wa-qāla li-qalbihi iṣbir
sentences.l: Then Qamar al-Zamān, when he-wanted to kiss-her on her-mouth, was-ashamed before God (the) Exalted, and-turned with-his-head, and-turned-aside his-face, and-said to-his-heart: Be-patient.
sentences.i: Then, as Qamar al-Zamān was about to kiss her on the mouth, he felt shame before God Most High; he turned his head and looked away, and said to his heart, “Be patient.”
sentences.n: The shadda of يقبّلها is the print's own. fī, “on”: “to kiss her on her mouth”. istaḥā min, “to be ashamed before”: the edition's spelling of istaḥyā, Form X, with a single yāʾ, a common spelling; min marks the one before whom one feels shame. taʿālā, “exalted be He”. dāra bi-raʾsihi, “he turned with his head”: bi- marks what is turned; the hamza of برأسه is printed. والفت is doubtful. It is read here as wa-alfata wajhahu, “and turned his face aside”, as if a Form IV of lafata, “to turn (aside)”, a form the dictionaries do not record in this sense; the print may rather mean wa-lafata wajhahu with a stray alif, or wa-iltafata, “and he turned”, with a tāʾ dropped, though that verb does not take wajhahu as its object. The sense is clear either way: he looked away. li-, “to”, marks the one addressed, his own heart. iṣbir, imperative of ṣabara, “be patient, hold out”.

sentences.t: فَتَفَكَّرَ فِي نَفْسِهِ وَقَالَ أَنَا أَصْبِرُ لِئَلَّا يَكُونَ وَالِدِي لَمَّا غَضِبَ عَلَيَّ وَحَبَسَنِى فِي هٰذَا الْمَوْضِعِ جَاءَ لِي بِهٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةِ وَأَمَرَهَا بِالنِّيَامِ بِجَانِبِى لِيَمْتَحِنَنِي بِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-tafakkara fī nafsihi wa-qāla anā aṣbiru li-allā yakūna wālidī lammā ghaḍiba ʿalayya wa-ḥabasanī fī hādhā al-mawḍiʿi jāʾa lī bi-hādhihi al-ṣabiyyati wa-amarahā bi-al-niyāmi bi-jānibī li-yamtaḥinanī bihā
sentences.l: And-he-reflected in himself and-said: I, I-will-be-patient, lest it-be (that) my-father, when he-was-angry with-me and-shut-me-up in this the-place, came to-me with-this the-girl and-ordered-her to-the-sleeping at-my-side, to-test-me with-her,
sentences.i: He thought it over and said to himself, “I will hold back, for it may be that my father, when he was angry with me and shut me up in this place, brought me this girl and told her to sleep beside me, to put me to the test with her;
sentences.n: The print has عضب, a misprint for غضب, corrected here: ghaḍiba ʿalayya, “he was angry with me”, the dot of the ghayn having dropped. The print has بجابنى, a misprint for بجانبى, corrected here: bi-jānibī, “at my side”, as bi-jānibihi in the last night; the ى is the edition's ى for final ي. tafakkara, Form V, “to reflect”. anā aṣbiru, “I will be patient”: the pronoun stands first for emphasis. li-allā, “lest, so that … not”, with the subjunctive yakūna: “lest it be that”, that is, “in case”; its ئ is printed. lammā ghaḍiba … wa-ḥabasanī, “when he was angry with me and shut me up”, is a clause of time set inside the sentence; the shadda of عليّ is the print's own, and حبسنى has ى for final ي. jāʾa lī bi-, “brought me”: jāʾa bi-, “to come with”, is “to bring”, and li- marks the one it is brought to. amara bi-, “to order (a thing)”: bi- marks what is ordered. bi-al-niyāmi, “to sleep”: niyām is a verbal noun of nāma, “to sleep”, a rarer twin of nawm that the dictionaries record. The shadda of الصبيّة is the print's own. imtaḥana, Form VIII, “to test”: bi- marks the means of the trial, “to test me with her”.

sentences.t: وَأَوْصَاهَا أَنِّي إِذَا نَبَّهْتُهَا لَا تَسْتَيْقِظْ سَرِيعًا وَقَالَ لَهَا أَيَّ شَيْءٍ فَعَلَ بِكِ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ فَأَعْلِمِينِي بِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-awṣāhā annī idhā nabbahtuhā lā tastayqiẓ sarīʿan wa-qāla lahā ayya shayʾin faʿala biki Qamaru al-Zamāni fa-aʿlimīnī bihi
sentences.l: and-charged-her that-I, when I-rouse-her, not she-is-to-wake quickly; and-said to-her: Whatever thing does to-you Qamar al-Zamān, then-inform-me of-it;
sentences.i: and charged her not to wake quickly when I tried to rouse her, and told her, ‘Whatever Qamar al-Zamān does to you, let me know of it.’
sentences.n: awṣā, Form IV, “to charge, instruct”. اني اذا نبّهتها is loosely built: it begins annī, “that I”, with himself as subject, goes on to a condition, idhā nabbahtuhā, “when I rouse her”, and ends with her, lā tastayqiẓ, “she is not to wake”. One would expect annahā, “that she”; the print is kept and read as it stands. The shadda of نبّهتها is the print's own: nabbaha, Form II, “to rouse”. lā with the jussive forbids. ayya shayʾin … fa-, “whatever thing … then”: ayy is used as a conditional and is the object of faʿala, and fa- brings in the answer; the shadda of ايّ is printed. faʿala bi-, “to do to”: bi- marks the one it is done to. aʿlama bi-, Form IV, “to inform of”: bi- marks the news; aʿlimīnī is a feminine imperative.

sentences.t: أَوْ يَكُونَ وَالِدِي وَاقِفًا مُسْتَخْفِيًا فِي مَكَانٍ بِحَيْثُ يَطَّلِعُ عَلَيَّ وَأَنَا لَا أَنْظُرُهُ وَهُوَ يَنْظُرُ جَمِيعَ مَا أَفْعَلُهُ بِهٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: aw yakūna wālidī wāqifan mustakhfiyan fī makānin bi-ḥaythu yaṭṭaliʿu ʿalayya wa-anā lā anẓuruhu wa-huwa yanẓuru jamīʿa mā afʿaluhu bi-hādhihi al-ṣabiyyati
sentences.l: or (lest) be my-father standing hiding-himself in a-place such-that he-looks-down on-me, and-I not I-see-him, and-he sees all what I-do with-this the-girl;
sentences.i: or my father may be standing hidden somewhere he can watch me, unseen by me while he sees everything I do with this girl;
sentences.n: aw yakūna, “or (lest) it be”, still hangs on li-allā, hence the subjunctive. wāqif, “standing”, and mustakhfī, “hiding oneself” (active participle of istakhfā, Form X), are accusative as the predicate of yakūna. bi-ḥaythu, “in such a way that”. yaṭṭaliʿu ʿalā, from iṭṭalaʿa, Form VIII, “to look down on, watch unseen”; the shadda of عليّ is printed. wa-anā …, wa-huwa …, “while I … while he …”: two circumstantial clauses. anẓuruhu and yanẓuru jamīʿa take their objects directly, “I see him”, “he sees all”, as in everyday speech, where Classical naẓara wants ilā. faʿala bi-, as above, “to do to”.

sentences.t: فَيُصْبِحُ يُوَبِّخُنِى وَيَقُولُ لِي كَيْفَ تَقُولُ مَالِي أَرَبٌ فِى الزَّوَاجِ وَأَنْتَ قَبَّلْتَ تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةَ وَعَانَقْتَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-yuṣbiḥu yuwabbikhunī wa-yaqūlu lī kayfa taqūlu mā-lī arabun fī al-zawāji wa-anta qabbalta tilka al-ṣabiyyata wa-ʿānaqtahā
sentences.l: And-he-will-be-in-the-morning rebuking-me, and-saying to-me: How (can) you-say, ‘Not-for-me (any) need in the-marriage,’ and-you kissed that the-girl and-embraced-her?
sentences.i: and in the morning he will reproach me and say, ‘How can you say you have no wish to marry, when you kissed that girl and held her in your arms?’
sentences.n: aṣbaḥa with an imperfect, “to be doing in the morning”: yuṣbiḥu yuwabbikhunī, “in the morning he will be scolding me”. The shadda of يوبّخنى is the print's own, and its ى is the edition's ى for final ي. مالي is set solid in the print: mā lī, “there is not for me”, pointed here across the join. arab, “need, wish”. فى is spelt with ى for final ي. wa-anta, “when you”, brings in a circumstantial clause. qabbala, Form II, “to kiss”; ʿānaqa, Form III, “to embrace”.

sentences.t: فَأَنَا أَكُفُّ نَفْسِي عَنْهَا لِئَلَّا يَنْكَشِفَ أَمْرِي مَعَ وَالِدِي
sentences.tr: fa-anā akuffu nafsī ʿanhā li-allā yankashifa amrī maʿa wālidī
sentences.l: So-I, I-restrain my-self from-her, lest be-uncovered my-affair with my-father.
sentences.i: So I will keep myself from her, so as not to be found out before my father.
sentences.n: kaffa nafsahu ʿan, “to restrain oneself from”: the shadda of اكفّ is printed. li-allā with the subjunctive yankashifa: inkashafa, Form VII, “to be laid bare”. amrī, “my affair”: his case, the truth about him.

sentences.t: وَالصَّوَابُ أَنِّي لَا أَلْمِسُ هٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةَ فِي تِلْكَ السَّاعَةِ وَلَا أَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهَا غَيْرَ أَنِّي آخُذُ لِي مِنْهَا شَيْأً يَكُونُ أَمَارَةً عِنْدِي وَتَذْكِرَةً لَهَا حَتَّى يَبْقَى بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَهَا إِشَارَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-al-ṣawābu annī lā almisu hādhihi al-ṣabiyyata fī tilka al-sāʿati wa-lā anẓuru ilayhā ghayra annī ākhudhu lī minhā shayʾan yakūnu amāratan ʿindī wa-tadhkiratan lahā ḥattā yabqā baynī wa-baynahā ishāratun
sentences.l: And-the-right-course (is) that-I not touch this the-girl in that the-hour, and-not look at-her, except that-I take for-me from-her a-thing (that) will-be a-token with-me and-a-reminder for-her, so-that remains between-me and-between-her a-sign.
sentences.i: The right course is for me not to touch this girl at this hour, nor even to look at her, except that I will take something of hers to keep by me as a token and to serve her as a reminder, so that there may be a sign between us.”
sentences.n: al-ṣawāb, “what is right, the proper course”. lamasa, “to touch”, imperfect yalmisu or yalmusu. The shadda of الصبيّة is the print's own. fī tilka al-sāʿati, “in that hour”: this very hour. ghayra anna, “except that, only”. ākhudhu lī, “I take for myself”: li- marks the one who benefits; the آ is printed. شيأ is the edition's spelling of shayʾan, as in the last night, with the hamza on an alif seat; the أ is printed. yakūnu amāratan, “(that) will be a token”, describes shayʾan without a relative pronoun, as after an indefinite noun. amāra, “sign, token”; tadhkira, “reminder, keepsake”; lahā, “for her”: li- marks the one to be reminded, since the missing ring will tell her someone has been there; “a keepsake of her” is a possible reading too. ḥattā, “so that”, with yabqā (a verb in -ā shows no change). baynī wa-baynahā, “between me and between her”: Arabic repeats bayna before each pronoun. ishāratun, “a sign”, is the subject of yabqā.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ رَفَعَ كَفَّ الصَّبِيَّةِ وَأَخَذَ مِنْ خِنْصِرِهَا خَاتَمًا يُسَاوِي جُمْلَةً مِنَ الْمَالِ لِأَنَّ فَصَّهُ كَانَ مِنْ نَفِيسِ الْجَوَاهِرِ وَمَنْقُوشٌ فِي دَائِرَتِهِ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni rafaʿa kaffa al-ṣabiyyati wa-akhadha min khinṣirihā khātaman yusāwī jumlatan mina al-māli li-anna faṣṣahu kāna min nafīsi al-jawāhiri wa-manqūshun fī dāʾiratihi hādhihi al-abyātu
sentences.l: Then Qamar al-Zamān raised (the) palm (of) the-girl, and-took from her-little-finger a-ring (that) equals a-sum of the-wealth, because its-stone was of (the) precious (of) the-jewels; and-engraved in its-circle (are) these the-verses:
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān lifted the girl's hand and took from her little finger a ring worth a great deal of money, for its stone was one of the costliest of jewels; and round its band these verses were engraved:
sentences.n: kaff, “palm, hand” (f.); the shadda of الصبيّة is the print's own. khinṣir, “the little finger”. sāwā, Form III, “to be equal to”, and so of goods, “to be worth”: yusāwī jumlatan mina al-māli, “it is worth a sum of money”, a large one. faṣṣ, the stone set in a ring. nafīs al-jawāhir, “the precious of jewels”: an adjective set before its noun in a construct, “the costliest gems”. ومنقوش has no accusative alif, so it is not a second predicate of kāna but begins a new clause, manqūshun … hādhihi al-abyātu, “engraved … (are) these verses”, with the predicate set first; a Classical writer might have kept it under kāna, wa-manqūshan. dāʾira, “circle”, here the hoop of the ring; its ئ is printed. abyāt, “verses”, plural of bayt.

sentences.t:
لَا تَحْسِبُوْا اِنِّي نَسِيتُ عُهُودَكُمْ * مَهْمَا اَطَلْتُمْ فِي الزَّمَانِ صُدُودَكُمْ
يَا سَادَتِي جُودُوْا عَلَيَّ وَاَعْطِفُوْا * فَعَسَى اُقَبِّلُ ثَغْرَكُمْ وَخُدُودَكُمْ
وَاللّٰهِ اِنِّي لَسْتُ اَبْرَحُ عَنْكُمُ * وَلَوِ اعْتَدَيْتُمْ فِي الْغَرَامِ حُدُودَكُمْ
sentences.tr:
lā taḥsibū innī nasītu ʿuhūdakum * mahmā aṭaltum fī al-zamāni ṣudūdakum
yā sādatī jūdū ʿalayya wa-aʿṭifū * fa-ʿasā uqabbilu thaghrakum wa-khudūdakum
wa-Allāhi innī lastu abraḥu ʿankumu * wa-lawi iʿtadaytum fī al-gharāmi ḥudūdakum
sentences.l:
Do-not reckon that-I have-forgotten your-pledges, * however-much you-have-prolonged in the-time your-turnings-away.
O my-lords, be-generous to-me and-be-kind, * so-perhaps I-may-kiss your-mouth and-your-cheeks.
By-God, I, not I-am-departing from-you, * even-if you-overstepped in the-passion your-bounds.
sentences.i:
Do not think I have forgotten the pledges between us, however long you go on turning away from me.
My masters, be generous to me and kind, and perhaps I may kiss your mouth and cheeks.
By God, I will never leave you, even though in this love you pass all bounds.
sentences.n: Metre: kāmil, rhyming in -ūdakum. The pointing is the print's own. The beloved is addressed in the plural, as often in love poetry, and called “my lords” (sādatī). Line 1: the print points اِنِّي, innī, where after ḥasiba, “to think”, one would expect annī, “that I”; kept. The sukūn on the wāw of تَحْسِبُوْا, as on جُودُوْا and وَاَعْطِفُوْا in line 2, is the print's way of marking the long vowel. ʿuhūd, “pledges, compacts”; mahmā, “however much”; ṣudūd, “turning away, aversion”. Line 2: jāda ʿalā, “to be generous to”. وَاَعْطِفُوْا is pointed as a Form IV, aʿṭifū, where ʿaṭafa, “to incline kindly”, is ordinarily Form I, iʿṭifū; the metre needs the syllable a-, so the print's form stands. ʿasā, “perhaps”, here with a bare imperfect: “perhaps I may kiss”. thaghr, “mouth”, properly the front teeth. Line 3: lastu abraḥu ʿankumu, “I am not leaving you”: bariḥa ʿan, “to leave, quit”; the printed ḍamma of عَنْكُمُ lengthens the pronoun for the metre. Allāh is printed with a dagger alif. wa-law, “even if”; iʿtadā, Form VIII, “to transgress”; ḥudūd, “bounds, limits”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ نَزَعَ ذٰلِكَ الْخَاتَمَ مِنْ خِنْصِرِ الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ وَلَبِسَهُ فِي خِنْصِرِهِ وَأَدَارَ ظَهْرَهُ إِلَيْهَا وَنَامَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni nazaʿa dhālika al-khātama min khinṣiri al-malikati Budūra wa-labisahu fī khinṣirihi wa-adāra ẓahrahu ilayhā wa-nāma
sentences.l: Then Qamar al-Zamān pulled-off that the-ring from (the) little-finger (of) the-Queen Budūr, and-put-it-on in his-little-finger, and-turned his-back to-her and-slept.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān drew the ring off Queen Budūr's little finger and put it on his own, turned his back on her and went to sleep.
sentences.n: nazaʿa, “to pull off”: the story goes back over the taking of the ring after the verses. al-malika, “the queen”: Budūr is a king's daughter, and the narrator gives her the royal title. labisa, “to put on, wear”, of a ring as of clothes; fī, “on”. adāra ẓahrahu ilā, “to turn one's back on”: adāra, Form IV, “to turn round”, and ilā, “towards”, marks the one it is turned on.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ الْجِنِّيَّةُ لَمَّا رَأَتْ ذٰلِكَ وَقَالَتْ لِدَهْنَشَ وَقَشْقَشَ هَلْ رَأَيْتُمَا مَحْبُوبِي قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَمَافَعَلَهُ مِنَ الْعِفَّةِ عَنْ هٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥat Maymūnatu al-jinniyyatu lammā raʾat dhālika wa-qālat li-Dahnasha wa-Qashqasha hal raʾaytumā maḥbūbī Qamara al-Zamāni wa-mā-faʿalahu mina al-ʿiffati ʿan hādhihi al-ṣabiyyati
sentences.l: And-rejoiced Maymūna the-jinniyya when she-saw that, and-said to-Dahnash and-Qashqash: Have you-two-seen my-beloved Qamar al-Zamān, and-what he-did of the-chastity from this the-girl?
sentences.i: Maymūna the jinniyya was glad when she saw this, and said to Dahnash and Qashqash, “Did you see my beloved Qamar al-Zamān, and the chaste restraint he showed towards this girl?
sentences.n: The shadda of الجنّية is the print's own here, and رأت has its hamza printed. li-, “to”, marks those addressed; Dahnash and Qashqash are diptotes, -a in the genitive. hal asks the question. raʾaytumā, “you two saw”, is dual. maḥbūb, “beloved”: Qamar al-Zamān is Maymūna's favourite. ومافعله is set solid in the print: wa-mā faʿalahu, “and what he did”, pointed here across the join. min, “of”, explains mā: “what he did by way of chastity”. ʿiffa ʿan, “abstaining from”.

sentences.t: فَهٰذَا مِنْ كَمَالِ مَحَاسِنِهِ فَانْظُرَا كَيْفَ رَأَى هٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةَ وَحُسْنَهَا وَجَمَالَهَا وَلَمْ يُعَانِقْهَا وَلَمْ يُقَبِّلْهَا وَلَا مَدَّ يَدَهُ إِلَيْهَا بَلْ أَدَارَ ظَهْرَهُ إِلَيْهَا وَنَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-hādhā min kamāli maḥāsinihi fa-unẓurā kayfa raʾā hādhihi al-ṣabiyyata wa-ḥusnahā wa-jamālahā wa-lam yuʿāniqhā wa-lam yuqabbilhā wa-lā madda yadahu ilayhā bal adāra ẓahrahu ilayhā wa-nāma
sentences.l: For-this (is) of (the) perfection (of) his-good-qualities. So-look-you-two how he-saw this the-girl and-her-beauty and-her-loveliness, and-not he-embraced-her, and-not he-kissed-her, and-not he-stretched his-hand to-her, but he-turned his-back to-her and-slept.
sentences.i: This comes of the perfection of his virtues. See how he looked on this girl in all her beauty and loveliness, and did not embrace her or kiss her or so much as reach out his hand to her, but turned his back on her and went to sleep.”
sentences.n: maḥāsin, “good qualities, charms”, a plural with no singular in use. min, “of”: this is part of his perfection. unẓurā is a dual imperative, to the two jinn. رأى has its hamza printed. lam with the jussive (yuʿāniq, yuqabbil) and lā with the perfect (lā madda) both deny the past; the second, after a denial already made, is the emphatic “nor did he so much as …”. bal, “rather, but”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَا لَهَا نَعَمْ قَدْ رَأَيْنَا مَا صَنَعَ مِنَ الْكَمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālā lahā naʿam qad raʾaynā mā ṣanaʿa mina al-kamāli
sentences.l: And-they-two-said to-her: Yes, we-have-seen what he-did of the-perfection.
sentences.i: “Yes,” they said to her, “we saw the perfect virtue he showed.”
sentences.n: qālā is dual: “the two of them said”. qad with the perfect, “indeed”. رأينا has its hamza printed. mā ṣanaʿa mina al-kamāli, “what he did of perfection”: min again explains mā.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ انْقَلَبَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ وَجَعَلَتْ نَفْسَهَا بُرْغُوثًا وَدَخَلَتْ ثِيَابَ بُدُورَ مَحْبُوبَةِ دَهْنَشَ وَمَشَتْ عَلَى سَاقِهَا وَطَلَعَتْ عَلَى فَخِذِهَا وَمَشَتْ تَحْتَ سُرَّتِهَا مِقْدَارَ أَرْبَعَةِ قَرَارِيطَ وَقَرَصَتْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika inqalabat Maymūnatu wa-jaʿalat nafsahā burghūthan wa-dakhalat thiyāba Budūra maḥbūbati Dahnasha wa-mashat ʿalā sāqihā wa-ṭalaʿat ʿalā fakhidhihā wa-mashat taḥta surratihā miqdāra arbaʿati qarārīṭa wa-qaraṣathā
sentences.l: So-at that, Maymūna changed-shape and-made herself a-flea, and-entered (the) clothes (of) Budūr, (the) beloved (of) Dahnash, and-walked on her-shank, and-climbed onto her-thigh, and-walked under her-navel (the) measure (of) four qīrāṭs, and-nipped-her.
sentences.i: At that Maymūna changed her shape and made herself into a flea, and crept into the clothes of Budūr, Dahnash's beloved. She walked up her leg and climbed onto her thigh, went on below her navel the length of four qīrāṭs, and bit her.
sentences.n: The print has وفرصتها, a misprint for وقرصتها, corrected here: wa-qaraṣathā, “and she nipped her”, with the dots of the qāf reduced to one; qaraṣa is the verb used of Dahnash as a flea at the start of the last night, and Maymūna now does to Budūr what he did to Qamar al-Zamān. fa-ʿinda dhālika, “so at that”. inqalaba, Form VII, “to be turned, change shape”. jaʿala nafsahā burghūthan, “she made herself a flea”: jaʿala takes two objects. dakhala takes its object directly: “entered her clothes”. maḥbūba, “beloved”: Budūr is Dahnash's favourite, as Qamar al-Zamān is Maymūna's; both names are diptotes. sāq, “shank, leg below the knee”. ṭalaʿa ʿalā, “to climb onto”. fakhidh, “thigh”. surra, “navel”. qīrāṭ (plural qarārīṭ, a diptote) is a twenty-fourth part of a whole, here probably of the cubit, so four of them make about a hand's breadth below the navel. miqdāra, “to the extent of”, is an accusative of measure.

sentences.t: فَفَتَحَتْ عَيْنَيْهَا وَاسْتَوَتْ قَاعِدَةً عَلَى حَيْلِهَا فَرَأَتْ شَابًّا نَائِمًا بِجَانِبِهَا وَهُوَ يَغِطُّ فِي نَوْمِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-fataḥat ʿaynayhā wa-istawat qāʿidatan ʿalā ḥaylihā fa-raʾat shābban nāʾiman bi-jānibihā wa-huwa yaghiṭṭu fī nawmihi
sentences.l: And-she-opened her-two-eyes, and-straightened-up sitting on her-strength, and-saw a-youth sleeping at-her-side, and-he snoring in his-sleep;
sentences.i: She opened her eyes and sat bolt upright, and saw a young man asleep beside her, snoring in his sleep,
sentences.n: ʿaynayhā, “her two eyes”, dual. istawā, Form VIII, “to straighten up”; qāʿidatan, “sitting”, is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). ʿalā ḥaylihā, “on her strength”, sitting right up, as Qamar al-Zamān did in the last night. The shadda of شابّا is the print's own; the أ of فرأت and the ئ of نائما are printed. bi-jānibihā, “at her side”. ghaṭṭa, yaghiṭṭu, “to snore, breathe heavily in sleep”.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ مِنْ أَجْمَلِ خَلْقِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَلَهُ لَوَاحِظُ تُخْجِلُ الْحُورَ الْحِسَانَ وَرِيقُهُ حُلْوُ الْمَذَاقِ وَأَنْفَعُ مِنَ التِّرْيَاقِ وَفَمٌ كَأَنَّهُ خَاتَمُ سُلَيْمَانَ وَشَفَتَانِ مِثْلَ لَوْنِ الْمَرْجَانِ وَخُدُودٌ كَشَقَائِقِ النُّعْمَانِ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِ بَعْضُ وَاصِفِيهِ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-huwa min ajmali khalqi Allāhi taʿālā wa-lahu lawāḥiẓu tukhjilu al-ḥūra al-ḥisāna wa-rīquhu ḥulwu al-madhāqi wa-anfaʿu mina al-tiryāqi wa-famun ka-annahu khātamu Sulaymāna wa-shafatāni mithla lawni al-marjāni wa-khudūdun ka-shaqāʾiqi al-nuʿmāni kamā qāla fīhi baʿḍu wāṣifīhi hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: and-he (was) of (the) most-beautiful (of the) creation (of) God (the) Exalted; and-to-him (were) glances (that) shame the-houris, the-lovely, and-his-spittle (was) sweet (of) the-taste and-more-beneficial than the-theriac, and-a-mouth as-if-it (were the) seal-ring (of) Solomon, and-two-lips like (the) colour (of) the-coral, and-cheeks like-(the)-anemones (of) al-Nuʿmān; as said about-him some (of) his-describers these the-verses:
sentences.i: and he was one of the most beautiful of God's creatures, with glances to put the lovely houris of Paradise to shame, spittle sweet to the taste and more healing than theriac, a mouth like Solomon's seal, lips the colour of coral, and cheeks like anemones, as one who described him said in these verses:
sentences.n: The portrait runs in rhymed prose (sajʿ) on -ān and -āq: ḥisān, madhāq, tiryāq, Sulaymān, marjān, nuʿmān. min, “of”: “one of the most beautiful”. wa-lahu, “and to him (were)”, “he had”, governs the whole list that follows, so famun, shafatāni and khudūdun are nominative. lawāḥiẓ, “glances”, plural of lāḥiẓ, the outer corner of the eye. akhjala, Form IV, “to put to shame”. al-ḥūr, “the houris”, the dark-eyed maidens of Paradise; ḥisān, “beautiful”. rīq, “saliva”, in love poetry the lover's sweet draught. ḥulw al-madhāq, “sweet of taste”. anfaʿ, “more beneficial”, elative, with min, “than”; tiryāq, theriac, the old antidote to poison. ka-anna, “as if”. khātam Sulaymān, the seal-ring of Solomon: the mouth is small and round as a signet. ka-, “like”, governs shaqāʾiq al-nuʿmān, the red anemone, said to be named after al-Nuʿmān, king of al-Ḥīra; the ئ of شقائق is printed. baʿḍu wāṣifīhi, “one of those who have described him”: wāṣifūna, “describers”, loses its nūn before the pronoun.

sentences.t:
سَلَى خَاطِرِي عَنْ زَيْنَبٍ وَنَوَارِي * بِوَرْدَةِ خَدٍّ فَوْقَ آسِ عِذَارِ
وَاَصْبَحْتُ بِالظَّبْيِ الْمُقَرْطَقِ مُغْرَمًا * وَلَا رَأْيَ لِي فِي عِشْقِ ذَاتِ سِوَارِ
اَنِيسِي فِي النَّادِي وَفِي خَلْوَتِي مَعًا * خِلَافَ اَنِيسِي فِي قَرَارَةِ دَارِي
فَيَا لَائِمِي فِي هَجْرِ هِنْدٍ وَزَيْنَبٍ * وَقَدْ لَاحَ عُذْرِي كَالصَّبَاحِ لِسَارِ
اَتَرْضَى بِاَنْ اَمْسَى اَسِيرَ اَسِيْرَةٍ * مُحَصَّنَةٍ اَوْ مِنْ وَرَاءِ جِدَارِ
sentences.tr:
salā khāṭirī ʿan Zaynabin wa-Nawārī * bi-wardati khaddin fawqa āsi ʿidhārī
wa-aṣbaḥtu bi-al-ẓabyi al-muqarṭaqi mughraman * wa-lā raʾya lī fī ʿishqi dhāti siwārī
anīsī fī al-nādī wa-fī khalwatī maʿan * khilāfa anīsī fī qarārati dārī
fa-yā lāʾimī fī hajri Hindin wa-Zaynabin * wa-qad lāḥa ʿudhrī ka-al-ṣabāḥi li-sārī
a-tarḍā bi-an amsā asīra asīratin * muḥaṣṣanatin aw min warāʾi jidārī
sentences.l:
Consoled-was my-mind from Zaynab and-Nawār * by-(the)-rose (of) a-cheek above (the) myrtle (of) a-line-of-down.
And-I-became with-the-fawn, the-tunic-clad, enamoured, * and-no inclination for-me in (the) love (of one) possessing a-bracelet.
My-companion in the-gathering and-in my-privacy together, * unlike my-companion in (the) depth (of) my-house.
So-O my-blamer for (the) forsaking (of) Hind and-Zaynab, * when has-shone my-excuse like-the-morning to-a-night-traveller:
Are-you-content that I-become (the) captive (of) a-captive-woman, * guarded, or from behind a-wall?
sentences.i:
My heart has forgotten Zaynab and Nawār for the rose of a cheek above a myrtle of down.
I have fallen in love with a fawn in a page's tunic, and have no mind to love one who wears a bracelet.
He is my companion in company and in private alike, not like the companion kept in the depths of my house.
You who blame me for forsaking Hind and Zaynab, when my excuse shines out like morning to one who travels by night:
would you have me become the captive of a captive, a woman kept guarded, or seen only from behind a wall?
sentences.n: Metre: ṭawīl, rhyming in -ārī. The pointing is the print's own. The poem prefers a youth to women, a common theme in the poetry of the period, and the narrator applies it to Qamar al-Zamān. Line 1: سَلَى is pointed salā, “to be consoled”, spelt with ى; salā ʿan, “to forget (someone)”: ʿan marks what is forgotten, and bi-, “by”, the consolation. Zaynab, Nawār and, in line 4, Hind are stock women's names of love poetry; Nawār takes a genitive -i with the rhyme vowel. The rose of the cheek lies above the myrtle (ās) of the ʿidhār, the line of first down on a youth's cheek, dark green against the red; the آ of آسِ is printed. Line 2: mughram bi-, “passionately in love with”: bi- marks the beloved. al-ẓaby al-muqarṭaq, “the fawn in a qurṭaq”, the short tunic worn by youths and pages. raʾy, “opinion”, here “inclination”; its hamza is printed. dhāt siwār, “she who wears a bracelet”, a woman. Line 3: anīsī, “my companion”: the youth goes with him to the nādī, the gathering, and into his privacy, while a wife is a companion only in qarārat al-dār, the inmost part of the house. khilāfa, “unlike”, an accusative used as a preposition. Line 4: lāʾim, “blamer”, the stock reproacher of love poetry; its ئ is printed. hajr, “forsaking”; lāḥa, “to gleam”. li-sārī, “to a night-traveller”: sārin, “one who travels by night”, with the rhyme vowel; li-, “to”, marks the one for whom the morning shines. Line 5: a-, the question; raḍiya bi-, “to be content with”: bi- marks what is accepted. an amsā, “that I become”: amsā, Form IV, properly “to be at evening”. asīr, “captive”, and asīra, a captive woman, one shut away in the harem; the print sets a sukūn on the yā of اَسِيْرَةٍ, marking the long vowel. muḥaṣṣana, “guarded, kept close”. muḥaṣṣana … aw min warāʾi jidār, “guarded … or from behind a wall”, echoes the Qurʾān (59:14), where muḥaṣṣana, “fortified”, and min warāʾi judurin, “from behind walls”, stand together: such a woman is met only behind walls; the ء of وَرَاءِ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَةَ بُدُورَ لَمَّا رَأَتْ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ أَخَذَهَا الْهُيَامُ وَالْوَجْدُ وَالْغَرَامُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malikata Budūra lammā raʾat Qamara al-Zamāni akhadhahā al-huyāmu wa-al-wajdu wa-al-gharāmu
sentences.l: Then the-Queen Budūr, when she-saw Qamar al-Zamān, took-her the-love-madness and-the-longing and-the-passion.
sentences.i: Then Queen Budūr, when she saw Qamar al-Zamān, was seized by love-madness, longing and passion.
sentences.n: inna puts al-malikata in the accusative, and the sentence restarts after lammā: akhadhahā, “(they) seized her”, with the feelings as subject. huyām, “love-madness”, passion that sends one wandering distracted; wajd, “ardent longing”; gharām, “consuming passion”. Two of the three near-synonyms, huyām and gharām, rhyme in -ām, in the manner of rhymed prose. رأت has its hamza printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
